lessons.title: Every time your cells build a big molecule, they make water. Why?
Starch and cellulose are both chains of glucose. Why can one feed you while the other builds a tree?

2.title: Lipids: triglycerides; Phospholipids, steroids and other lipids

lessons.title: Why is butter solid but olive oil runny, when both are made of the same kind of molecule?
Oily molecules avoid water, yet they wrap every cell in a thin film. How does that film build itself?

3.title: Protein structure and function; Amino acids and peptide bonds

lessons.title: Every protein in your body is built from just twenty building blocks. How can so few make so many?
A protein is only a chain of amino acids. So how does it fold into the exact shape its job needs?

11.title: How enzymes work; Enzyme inhibition and metabolic control; Factors affecting enzyme activity

lessons.title: Is an enzyme a rigid lock waiting for one key, or does it change shape as its target arrives?
Why does warming an enzyme speed it up, until suddenly it hardly works at all?
How can a single molecule switch off one reaction among the thousands running in a cell?

12.title: Enzymes in medicine and industry; Cloning and biotechnology; Prokaryotic cells and viruses

lessons.title: How can a cheap paper strip measure the sugar in a single drop of blood?
Why would a factory lock its enzymes in place when free enzymes work faster?
How can a tank of tiny living cells make medicines, cheese and even clean up oil spills?
A bacterium has no nucleus. So where does it keep its genes, and what else does it manage without?
A virus cannot feed, grow or divide. So how does one virus become millions?

16.title: Eukaryotic cell ultrastructure; Membrane structure (fluid mosaic)

lessons.title: A cell's outer membrane is just two molecules thick. Why do its molecules form that sheet by themselves?
How can you show that the molecules in a membrane never stop moving?
A plant cell shares most of its parts with yours. So what does it have that yours lacks, and why?

17.title: Protein secretion and the endomembrane system; Cell theory, microscopes and magnification

lessons.title: How can you measure the length of a cell you can only see through a microscope?
If you can enlarge an image as much as you like, why do some things inside a cell stay blurred?

lessons.title: To study one part of a cell, you first have to smash the cell open. How do you get that part out undamaged?

Cut open an organ or slice it thin: how do you know what you are looking at?
